items.title: Jensen Huang Says He Would Be 'Honoured' to Return as Nvidia CEO Amid Alleged Spy Affair Probe

items.summary: Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang is scheduled to appear before the United States' House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee in a closed-door transcribed interview on 1 December. This follows his resignation as CEO of the chip giant following reported extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter will sit for a similar closed-door transcribed interview a day later on 2 December. Republican representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford — chairs of the Foreign Affairs, China Select, and Intelligence Committees respectively — issued a press release stating they look forward to hearing from Huang and Teter regarding their roles in a potential breach of national security, emphasizing that the American people need answers on Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access advanced chips. The US bans the sale of its most advanced chips to China as part of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to lead AI; this measure came under former President Joe Biden, who signed the CHIPS Act into law. Under the Trump administration, Huang lobbied the US to relax export controls on chips to China through several meetings with President Donald Trump, and Trump eventually allowed the export of Nvidia's more powerful H200 chips to China in exchange for 25% of the revenue. On Monday, the US Commerce Department unveiled new restrictions that will make it harder for some countries — such as China, Russia, and Iran — to access the most advanced artificial intelligence chips through data centres located in other countries.
items.title: Jensen Huang to Face US Congressional Interviews on Nvidia's China Sales

items.summary:
Former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang made his first public remarks since resigning last week, stating Tuesday that he would be willing to return to lead the chipmaker if its board of directors asked him to do so. In a statement, Huang said: "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." The 63-year-old also acknowledged mistakes in his personal life, expressing regret over problems his conduct had caused the board. He said: "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life... I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret." Huang stated he owns his mistakes completely and is committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation.

Huang noted he had received widespread support following his departure, including calls from Nvidia employees, investors, business partners, and customers urging him to return. He added: "Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics," describing NVIDIA as "a once-in-a-generation company." His remarks came a day after reports suggested the board was not considering his reinstatement.

Nvidia announced Huang's resignation Thursday after 33 years as CEO, following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged relationship with a woman suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence. The chipmaker appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and began searching for a permanent successor. Following his departure, calls for his return have grown among investors and prominent technology executives. An online petition calling for his reinstatement has attracted more than 180,000 signatures, drawing support from figures including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. US President Donald Trump also expressed support Monday for Huang's possible return, saying he believed the former Nvidia chief had "learned a big lesson."
items.title: Jensen Huang Says He Would Be 'Honored' to Return as Nvidia CEO If Board Asks

items.summary: Canada's auto sector has become a central stress test for Ottawa amid US tariffs on the industry, prompting Prime Minister Mark Carney to signal that China could be part of the solution. Speaking while visiting Cambodia ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Carney said Canadian automakers might turn to European and Asian carmakers if no trade deal with the United States materialized, adding that Canada would move forward regardless. He had also met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing for their second face-to-face meeting in under a year, discussing closer relations and agreeing to further tariff cuts, though neither side addressed vehicles directly—although analysts believe it was prominent on both sides' agendas. Earlier this year, Canada announced it would admit 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at low tariffs, with plans to raise the quota gradually to 70,000 by 2030; a significant departure from the United States, which heavily tariffs Chinese EVs to protect domestic manufacturing. This move came as American tariffs on Canadian-made vehicle imports have caused thousands of job losses and anxiety over the sector's future, given that roughly 90% of cars built in Canada are shipped to and sold in the US. China has meanwhile viewed Canada as a potential entry point into the North American EV market, with manufacturers like BYD and Chery already lobbying for access. Last week, Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu toured a Chery plant in China and said Canadians could expect affordable Chinese EVs by early 2027. The toll of US tariffs has intensified as Stellantis announced it would sell its assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario—which had been idle since 2023 for planned retooling but became permanently shut down after Trump's tariffs; Canadian media reported that the company was considering leasing back 25% of the facility to assemble affordable EVs. The idea is unpopular with Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who warned against allowing Chinese EV kits to be assembled at Brampton in a letter to Carney. Lynette Ong, director of the China Governance Lab at the University of Toronto, cautioned that introducing Chinese auto manufacturing would be controversial due to fears over job losses and erosion of the North American industry, emphasizing the need for Canadian hiring, training, and technology transfer. Carney noted clear guardrails in Canada's dealings with China, including barring work on sensitive matters such as artificial intelligence and critical minerals, while Canada also pursues associate membership with the EU and a free trade deal with the Philippines—though how far Ottawa embraces Chinese manufacturing ultimately depends on ongoing US-Canada trade talks.
items.title: Carney Looks to China as Trump Tariffs Squeeze Canada's Car Industry

items.summary:
A French consumer association known as Halte à l'obsolescence programmée (HOP) announced Tuesday that the Paris prosecutor's office has decided to pursue Apple over alleged practices obstructing repairs and refurbishment of iPhones outside Apple's authorized service network. The trial is scheduled for June 2027, with a preliminary hearing set for February 25, 2027, to establish the schedule.

The case concerns 24 iPhone models and follows a complaint filed by HOP on December 7, 2022. At its center is a practice called "serialization," which links serial numbers of device components—such as screens, batteries, and cameras—to the phone. HOP alleges that this system can cause malfunctions when parts are replaced by repairers outside Apple's authorized network, including when genuine replacement parts are used without approval from the company's software.

The association says serialization limits independent repair options and makes it harder for consumers to have devices repaired outside Apple's service network. However, HOP noted that Apple had announced steps since 2022 to limit serialization on newer iPhones and allow some third-party repairs to be validated—though the effectiveness of these changes remains unconfirmed over time.
items.title: Apple to Face Trial in France Over Alleged Planned Obsolescence of iPhones

items.summary: This article opens a series exploring Shenzhen's transformation from a small fishing village into one of China's leading innovation centers in just over four decades. Bert Hofman, former World Bank country director for China, Mongolia and Korea, set out to find answers by examining the city's history, industries and the choices made by the people who shaped its journey. What is striking about Shenzhen is not only how far it has come but how it continually reinvents itself — moving from being known as the 'world's factory' to the 'Silicon Valley of hardware,' and now positioning itself as a hub for innovation and R&D. The piece frames these developments against the broader question of what has driven this remarkable transformation, inviting readers into an investigation of the forces behind Shenzhen's rise.
items.title: Shenzhen: The Making of a Miracle (Part 1)

items.summary: In this second installment exploring Shenzhen's transformation into what is often called a miracle city, the narrative frames the metropolis as a place where science fiction begins to take shape. Zak Dychtwald, author of Young China, serves as the guide for the piece, describing Shenzhen as a location where futuristic visions start becoming reality. The article positions the city at the forefront of technological development, noting that it is home to major tech companies including DJI, Huawei and Tencent, which are described collectively as giants shaping the next generation of technology. Through visits ranging from a university robotics arena to an AI startup, Dychtwald examines one central question: what lies ahead for a city already engaged in building the future. The piece conveys Shenzhen's identity not through statistics or historical detail but through its concentration of innovation and young talent, presenting it as a living laboratory where emerging technologies are actively taking form.
items.title: Shenzhen: The Making of a Miracle (Part 2)

items.summary:
On Tuesday, Iran fired drones at a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain — the host nation of the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet — marking its third attack in recent days on American military targets there after roughly a two-month lull in fighting that began Feb. 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran, now in its eighth month. Bahrain said it issued an alert about the incoming fire and that its air defense systems intercepted what officials called "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks," while both the U.S. military and Bahrain reported no damage to equipment or injury to American personnel. The strikes followed earlier Friday and Sunday attacks on a U.S. early warning radar facility and a radar system at an American helicopter base in Bahrain, though little or no damage appeared to result from those too.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said the retaliation was aimed at continued aggression against Iran's airspace and the use of regional bases for hostile acts, framing it as a response to U.S. attacks on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations. The moves have drawn condemnations across the region: Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each denounced the Bahrain attack as a violation of its sovereignty and a threat to stability.

Analysts attribute Iran's growing impatience partly to mounting economic pressure from a U.S.-enforced naval blockade in and around the Strait of Hormuz — described as crucial for the world's energy supplies, where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began. The blockade has curtailed Iranian crude exports while oil tankers moving under U.S. military protection helped return Gulf shipments to roughly prewar levels. Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi said the attacks may signal a strategic shift after months of waiting for an attack before retaliating against base operational capability, and Hamidreza Azizi of the International Crisis Group wrote that Iranian leaders are weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation." Bahrain-based defense analyst Sascha Bruchmann cautioned not to overestimate what was seen in Bahrain this week.

President Donald Trump has remained circumspect about next steps, saying new strikes are highly unlikely while sending a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — telling VP JD Vance that talks aren't needed. The arrival of USS Theodore Roosevelt's strike group means combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea and Mediterranean now exceed those deployed when the war began; Israel's Institute for National Security Studies says this adds offensive firepower and missile interception capacity alongside USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington carriers.

Iran has also continued attacking ships transiting key waterways: on Tuesday UKMTO reported a tanker attacked twice north of Oman with a second strike causing fire, plus a cargo vessel off Yemen that repelled an attempted boarding; Iran's Fars news agency reported two ships struck by mines in the Strait of Hormuz. In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthis have solidified control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait after an anti-Houthi coalition force allied with the Saudi-backed government retreated over the weekend.

Despite intensified mediation from Qatar — whose Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari warned that escalation posed "an extremely grave danger" to reaching an agreement — negotiations remain stalled. Iranian officials describe the situation as "no war, no peace," while adviser Mahdi Mohammadi framed U.S. economic pressure as an effort to engineer a domestic security crisis; Tehran says it is open to a deal but signals readiness to escalate amid tightening sanctions and blockade.
items.title: Iran Launches Third Round of Strikes on Bahrain; U.S. Expands Gulf Naval Presence Amid Stalled War Talks

items.summary: The piece opens with a standard site notice confirming that browsing agrees to updated cookie use, Privacy Policy and Terms of Use, while noting that users can adjust their settings through their browser. It then frames its central theme as 'Driving the Future,' describing how, across Asia, countries and individuals are collaborating to realize shared dreams in the present moment. Through personal stories, the article explores how technology, cooperation and a firm belief in sharing progress are converging to reshape the continent. Its featured example is Singapore, where Chinese autonomous technology is being tested on city streets with hopes of improving daily convenience and safety. The cars involved carry advanced sensors capable of even detecting an occasional chicken crossing the road while changing lanes safely and promptly. Extensive testing aims to help these driverless taxis adapt to local conditions and reach the competence of a seasoned Singaporean taxi driver.
items.title: Assignment Asia: Driving the Future

items.summary: Wang Yan of CGTN frames universities as catalysts for shared prosperity, reviewing a forum that opened the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) process ahead of its 2026 host year. The event was co-hosted by Tsinghua University and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), with support from the Association of Pacific Rim Universities, drawing more than 300 delegates from 61 universities across 24 countries and regions, including representatives from 14 APEC economies and 10 other countries. Its theme—"Open, Innovative, Collaborative: Universities as Catalysts for Asia-Pacific's Prosperous Future"—echoed the broader APEC 2026 theme of "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together." The forum examined higher education in the AI era, moving from knowledge to impact, rethinking computer science alongside the humanities, and building collaborative innovation ecosystems. Wang Yan argues that universities serve as catalysts for prosperity amid rapid technological shifts and sustainability challenges, with openness at their core. She notes Shenzhen's transformation from a "cultural desert" into a national model of urban cultural development and a "city of libraries," citing 1,227 library service points, seven major book stores, and a collection exceeding 68 million volumes as evidence of that shift. In education, she contends openness takes the form of academic mobility, mutual recognition of qualifications, joint research, and cross-border collaboration backed by working infrastructure rather than rhetoric—goals enshrined in the APEC Education Strategy, described as the first such blueprint stretching to 2030 since APEC's founding in 1989. On innovation, Tsinghua University President Li Luming characterizes the era's challenge as "cognitive sovereignty," defined as the capacity to ask new questions, venture into uncharted territory, and resist outsourcing thinking entirely to a model; he asserts that technology determines how far societies can go while the humanities guide where they should. Wang Yan stresses that no single university or economy can build industrial capability alone, making cooperation essential. She points to Tsinghua's long-standing industry-university-research integration as a strategic pillar and highlights CUHK-Shenzhen—founded in 2014 by The Chinese University of Hong Kong in partnership with Shenzhen University—as an example of how institutions from different systems can multiply rather than dilute their strengths, located at the forum's venue within the Greater Bay Area. Concluding on people as the ultimate drivers of future decisions, she underscores that while AI may power the economy, only education can empower its people.
items.title: Universities as Catalysts for Shared Prosperity in the Asia-Pacific: APEC 2026 University Leaders' Forum

items.summary:
The European Union and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) could be heading for a breakthrough year in 2027, when the two sides mark 50 years of diplomatic ties. A long-awaited trade agreement with Indonesia is expected to take effect, while a deal with the Philippines is nearing completion and negotiations with Thailand and Malaysia are making progress. By the end of next year, the EU could have trade deals in place with six Southeast Asian states, up from just two today.

The anniversary could also revive the long-standing ambition of a broader trade agreement between the EU and ASEAN. On November 17, the European Commission hosted a dialogue in Brussels to discuss trade relations with Southeast Asia, including progress on existing and pending free trade agreements (FTAs).

"Finalizing FTAs is only the beginning, not the end," Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, told DW. "Unfortunately, in many cases, this is where there is a failure." Communication and training are key, he said.

The hard work begins after signing. For Brussels, the priority should now be to tackle the less conspicuous obstacles to trade. Cutting customs delays, simplifying regulations, and helping smaller European businesses enter unfamiliar Southeast Asian markets will determine whether an FTA succeeds. "European companies with little or no experience in Southeast Asia would benefit from greater on-the-ground support, particularly practical, firsthand guidance on informal business practices and the unwritten local rules," Alfred Gerstl, an associate professor at Palacky University Olomouc in the Czech Republic, told DW.

One option is to expand the assistance offered by European chambers of commerce, trade delegations, and EU offices in Southeast Asia. This could range from helping firms find distributors to explaining local licensing requirements and how to qualify for preferential tariffs. In Vietnam, for instance, sustained pressure from Brussels has helped improve market access for European pharmaceutical firms.

In Indonesia, the EU has worked on trade facilitation while pressing Jakarta over import restrictions and halal certification requirements, said Camille Nessel, a researcher at the Universite Libre de Bruxelles. Regular consultations with businesses on both sides could also help Brussels spot problems before they become trade disputes.

Trade policy has also acquired a geopolitical purpose in Brussels. "If trade policy is expected to reduce strategic dependencies, we are asking it to deliver on objectives that remain insufficiently defined, let alone demonstrating how to achieve them," Nessel told DW.

The EU wants to reduce its dependence on a handful of suppliers for the minerals needed for batteries and other clean technologies, while Southeast Asian producers, particularly Indonesia, want foreign investors to help develop domestic processing industries rather than merely buy raw materials. The EU and Indonesia have already clashed over Jakarta's restrictions on nickel exports. European investment in processing facilities, agreements on environmental standards, and greater regulatory certainty would give both sides concrete gains, said Nessel.

"The real value of an FTA is not just opening a market but giving the EU the leverage to keep it open," she added.

Pasha Hsieh, Lee Kong Chian Professor of Law and Jean Monnet Chair at Singapore Management University, said Brussels should prioritize ratifying its investment protection agreements with Singapore and Vietnam. Signed in 2018 and 2019, respectively, the agreements still require ratification by all EU member states before entering into force.

"These delays underline the need to follow through on negotiated commitments," Hsieh said. The issue is particularly relevant as the EU looks to develop investment protocols in other Southeast Asian states where investors have sometimes faced uncertainty over legal protections. Indonesia, for instance, has terminated numerous bilateral investment treaties, including agreements with the Netherlands and Spain.

A larger question is whether the EU should continue pursuing bilateral deals with Southeast Asian countries or revive its original ambition of a region-to-region agreement with ASEAN. The EU and ASEAN launched negotiations for a region-wide FTA in 2007 but suspended them two years later amid disagreements over wide economic disparities among ASEAN members and political concerns. Technical discussions resumed in 2017, but little has come of them.

ASEAN already has regional agreements with China and several other economies. Beijing upgraded its free trade agreement with ASEAN in October 2025. Region-to-region frameworks extend beyond trade. Humphrey called for negotiations to begin on a region-to-region Digital Trade Agreement and Investment Protection Agreement. The EU-Singapore Digital Trade Agreement, which entered into force in February 2026, offers a possible model for wider cooperation.

"European businesses have long complained of operating at a disadvantage due to the lack of a region-to-region deal." It is high time that both sides elevated their ambitions and embraced the idea of working towards such an agreement, Humphrey said. The 2027 anniversary would be a convenient deadline for agreeing on what comes next, but Gerstl warned against mistaking another round of diplomatic ceremony for progress.

"There is a risk that attention will focus almost exclusively on the 2027 summit in Singapore and that the group photo will become the defining image of the event, only for momentum to fade in the years that follow," he added.
items.title: EU-ASEAN trade ties show progress but face informal barriers ahead of 2027 anniversary

items.summary:
A suspension of a Sydney-based logistics company has left nearly $500,000 worth of niche underwater equipment stuck somewhere within importer Tim Hochgrebe's supply chain with no clear path to retrieval. Hochgrebe, who owns the Byron Bay business, is dealing with the fallout from Top Logistics Australia, whose depot licences were cancelled in September by the Australian Border Force (ABF). Goods he expected within six weeks had still not arrived five months later; his replacement handler has an email address but no phone number, and contact attempts have failed. Hochgrebe said the ABF cancellation forced his Chinese-based shipping agent to find another Australian freight company, which now handles his goods with only limited reachability.

The delays trace back to a broader crackdown on illicit products that logistics experts say is slowing supply chains across Australia as the Christmas trade period begins. Businesses awaiting imported goods report trade and cash-flow problems; Business NSW's Jane Laverty noted small businesses are struggling to absorb delay costs, refunds, reputational damage and cash-flow strain.

The disruption centres on a court case: Top Logistics director Peter Ping Xie is due in Burwood Local Court on November 18, charged with dishonestly obtaining financial gain by deception over the alleged importation of illicit tobacco and vapes into Australia. Freight policy general manager Tom Jensen said border holds on some containers had blown out from one or two days to more than 30 days since December, tying up innocent imports flagged for inspection.

ABF data in its 2025/2026 annual report shows sea cargo cleared within five days fell by almost 2 per cent, to 91.6 per cent of the five-year average. The ABC understands all consignments held by Top Logistics Australia have been cleared or transferred to other licensed depots for storage and processing, with ABF notices advising owners, brokers and forwarders to locate and retrieve their goods.

Victorian-based importer Phil Burn reported nine remote-control lawn mowers worth $9,000 awaiting customs release; forced by excessive delays he had personally refunded the purchase cost of every mower while unable to locate them. He said relying on Chinese suppliers for logistics worked when things ran smoothly but became impossible to navigate during disruptions.
items.title: Nearly $500k of underwater gear in limbo after depot suspended amid illicit-product crackdown disrupting Australian supply chains

items.summary: Rights groups have raised alarms over a rising number of executions in Saudi Arabia. According to an AFP tally reported on Monday, the two most recent executions—those of Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani, both convicted of terrorist offenses—brought the total number of people executed in Saudi Arabia in 2026 to 211. Of these, 126 were convicted of drug trafficking and 17 on terrorism-related charges; 100 were Saudi nationals while the rest were foreign nationals. Human Rights Watch reported additional cases: five Ethiopian migrants executed for nonviolent drug-related offenses in July, two Bangladeshi nationals in October, and another Saudi national, Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, executed on October 17 for alleged offenses committed when he was a minor. Ahmed Benchemsi, Human Rights Watch's MENA spokesperson, told DW that in 2025 at least 356 people were executed—a record high—and that executions have continued at a high rate in 2026; Saudi Arabia has executed more than 2,000 people in the past decade. The Death Penalty Information Center ranks Saudi Arabia third in executions after China and Iran, consistent with earlier Amnesty International findings placing it as the world's third-most prolific executioner between 2022 and 2025. Comprehensive global data for 2026 are not yet available, and many countries treat execution numbers as state secrets. The two main methods of execution in Saudi Arabia are stoning or beheading, though death sentences are often issued as discretionary ta'zir rulings under which little to no information about the execution or fate of bodies is provided.
items.title: Saudi Arabia's Rising Executions Amid Regional Tensions and Rights Concerns

items.summary: After disappearing from Chad by the late 1980s and being declared extinct in the wild globally in 2000, the scimitar-horned oryx has regained a foothold through a reintroduction program led by the NGO Sahara Conservation. The species’ conservation status has improved to “endangered,” with its population in Ouadi Rimé–Ouadi Achim Wildlife Reserve—Chad’s largest protected area—growing from 25 individuals in 2016 to 700 today, making it the largest herd in the world. Despite this progress, the oryx continues to face challenges, including climate change impacts such as prolonged droughts and shifting conditions, as well as competition from livestock for grazing lands.
items.title: The scimitar-horned oryx is back in Chad

items.summary: A Georgia O'Keeffe painting hidden inside a closet for four decades is going up for auction on November 17 at Christie's in New York. The work, titled Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I, dates from 1930 and belongs to a series of three studies of the Lobo Mountain landscape in New Mexico; it was purchased April 15, 1963 — believed by its owner Betsy to be a gift from her grandparents on her aunt's graduation. It originally cost $3,800 (about $42,000 today adjusted for inflation), and Christie's estimates its current value at between $3 million and $5 million.
items.title: Georgia O'Keeffe's Long-Lost Painting Rediscovered and Set for Auction in New York

items.summary:
Jensen Huang, Nvidia's former chief executive who resigned last week amid revelations of extramarital affairs that intensified scrutiny of the company's China business, said on Tuesday he 'would be honored' to return as CEO if the board decided his comeback served shareholders and employees best. In his first public statement since resigning on November 12 over disclosures involving a relationship with Alice Huang — whom US intelligence agencies suspect has links to Chinese intelligence — Huang cited an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners and customers urging his return. He took responsibility for the problems he created at the board and committed to cooperating with its independent investigation.

In response to the crisis, which had erased more than $400 billion from Nvidia's market value by Monday's close, the company established a new board-level committee to oversee national security and export controls — its first major governance move since Huang left. The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former Goldman Sachs vice chair, with directors Stephen Neal of law firm Cooley and John Dabiri, a Caltech professor, also serving on it. The committee plans to meet at least quarterly, including in executive sessions, and will oversee Nvidia's national security and global trade compliance programs while working with independent legal, national security and trade-compliance experts.

Interim CEO Colette Kress will continue overseeing day-to-day operations during the transition. US President Donald Trump welcomed the move as a good idea for establishing a robust framework to safeguard national security while supporting technological innovation. The committee's creation came a day after the Trump administration announced further restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips from companies including Nvidia, coinciding with Trump heading to China for talks with Xi Jinping.

Nvidia has long sought to curb Beijing's access to its most advanced processors, placing the company's China business at the center of tensions over national security and US technological leadership — even as Chinese firms have repeatedly found ways around restrictions. Huang had previously advocated allowing more chip exports to China. Nvidia noted that major technology companies including Alphabet, Apple, Meta and Microsoft maintain board committees overseeing areas such as regulatory compliance, cybersecurity, privacy and strategy, whereas its new panel has a narrower mandate focused on national security — a structure more commonly associated with aerospace and defense firms.

The company also warned chip buyers in recent months that the proposed US Remote Access Security Act could expose Nvidia and its customers to legal risks by expanding Washington's oversight of Chinese companies' access to AI chips through cloud services. Huang's daughter Madison Huang, who is a senior director of product marketing at Nvidia, was closely involved in shaping the public defense of the company's ties to Megaspeed — which has been under investigation over possible diversion of restricted Nvidia chips to China and potential export-control violations; the firm denies wrongdoing.

Nvidia did not have a chief compliance officer according to its 2026 proxy statement, and it was unclear whether the committee was created in response to the revelations about Huang's affairs. The company is due to report third-quarter earnings after the market closes on Tuesday.
items.title: Nvidia's Huang Signals Willingness to Return as CEO; Board Sets Up National Security Panel

items.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos donated approximately $198.9 million in shares—771,492 Amazon shares—to nonprofit organizations on Monday, November 16, per an SEC Form 4 filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The latest contribution raised his total Amazon stock donations for 2026 to at least 2.44 million shares worth approximately $629.1 million. This year's giving followed two earlier rounds: 1,253,797 shares on May 1 and May 4, plus another 415,580 shares on August 25 and 26. The most recent donation comprised transfers of 674,088 Amazon shares on November 12 and 97,404 shares on November 13, both described as contributions to non-profit organizations. While the filing did not identify recipients, a separate SEC filing by the Bezos Earth Fund Foundation confirmed it received the 97,404 shares transferred on November 13; the remaining 674,088 shares' recipients have not been publicly identified. The combined value of donated shares was calculated using Amazon's closing price of $257.75 on November 16. Even after these transfers, Bezos holds more than 878 million Amazon shares directly—valued at approximately $226.4 billion based on Monday's closing stock price—and an additional 5,087,266 shares indirectly through trusts and a limited liability company he serves as trustee of but has disclaimed beneficial ownership of. The transfers represented about 0.09 percent of the Amazon shares Bezos directly held before donating. Forbes estimated his net worth at $376.7 billion as of Monday evening, placing him second on its Real-Time Billionaires list behind Elon Musk. Separately, Bezos and wife Lauren Sanchez Bezos made significant charitable contributions in 2025, with the couple's estimated donations reaching $600 million; their combined lifetime charitable contributions stood at approximately $4.7 billion through end of 2025, placing them tenth on Forbes' list of America's top 25 philanthropists. Bezos' giving also includes climate and nature initiatives: in 2020 he pledged $10 billion through the Bezos Earth Fund to combat climate change and protect nature by 2030; the fund has awarded approximately $2.4 billion in grants so far, and his Day One Fund's Day 1 Families Fund awarded $102.5 million to 32 organizations in 2025. His former wife MacKenzie Scott has donated billions since their 2019 divorce—$7.2 billion in 2025 alone, more than any other philanthropist worldwide and the largest annual amount Forbes tracked since it began tracking major donors in 2012; by end of 2025 she had given away approximately 46 percent of her estimated net worth. Scott donated $26.4 billion to more than 2,500 organizations between their divorce and end of 2025, placing her third on Forbes' list of America's top 25 philanthropists; recent gifts include $70 million to the American Indian College Fund in October, plus donations this year totaling $70 million each to Meals on Wheels America and Elizabeth City State University, and $20 million to youth mental health nonprofit Active Minds.
items.title: Jeff Bezos's $198.9M Amazon Share Donation and Comparisons with Other Philanthropists

items.summary: Users of Apple and Google services reported widespread difficulties accessing core digital platforms during a coordinated outage. Complaints centered on iCloud, the App Store, Wallet, Gmail, Google Search (with connection errors and sign-in failures), Apple Pay, and account verification logins. According to Downdetector, reports of service disruptions began climbing around 11:30 am ET (10:00 pm IST) and surged to nearly 1,500-2,000 within an hour. Affected users documented the problems on X, noting issues with messaging, emails, payments, fund transfers, and Apple iCloud account verification sign-ins.
items.title: Apple and Google Outage Disrupts App Store, Gmail, Search and Other Services

items.summary:
The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) plans to send property tax payment reminders via WhatsApp Business and Google Messages, with each message including a link for instant payment in an effort to boost collection. These messages will reach all 11,18,971 properties under the BMC's jurisdiction—either registered numbers or authorised representatives such as housing society secretaries—and implementation is expected to take a couple of months after a work order is issued. The Tax Assessment and Collection Department floated a tender for this messaging system, which M/s Vidarbha Infotech Pvt Ltd won as the lowest bidder at Rs 2.09 crore; the proposal was set to be tabled before the standing committee that week for approval. Vishwas Shankarwar, Deputy Municipal Commissioner in charge of Assessment and Collection, explained that reminders would initially go only to already-registered numbers while the contractor compiles data on remaining properties.

On revenue performance, Shankarwar noted the BMC had collected 50% of its annual property tax target of Rs 8,200 crore. For the previous financial year, however, the corporation achieved an all-time high collection of Rs 7,610 crore—surpassing its target through updated assessment policies, penalty recoveries and a strong late-March surge. Contextually, octroi historically accounted for roughly 35% of the BMC's total annual revenue but was abolished in 2017 with the introduction of GST, after which property tax became the civic body's highest source of revenue generation.
items.title: BMC's WhatsApp and Google Messages Property Tax Reminder System; Revenue Progress Under Octroi Abolition

items.summary: Police in Dhar, Madhya Pradesh arrested a man on charges of allegedly harassing his wife and her family by creating two fake Instagram accounts through which he sent obscene messages and objectionable photographs. The suspect was identified as Ankit Kasera (30) of Vivekananda Colony in Jaora, Ratlam district. According to police, the woman lodged a complaint at Manawar police station alleging that an unidentified person had been sending abusive messages and objectionable photographs via fake Instagram accounts. During investigation, Manawar police assisted by Dhar Cyber Cell traced the accounts to Kasera using technical evidence. Police said the suspect is the complainant's husband, with a dowry harassment case between them pending before a Manawar court. Investigators believe he created the accounts to pressure and defame his wife amid the ongoing dispute. The operation was conducted under the supervision of SP Sachin Sharma, ASP Vijay Dawar, SDOP Ramsingh Rathore and Inspector Rajesh Yadav, with assistance from Head Constable Aamir Ansari, constables Jitendra Kushwaha, Kamal Solanki and Prashant, and Head Constables Sarvesh and Mukesh. Police also seized two Android mobile phones allegedly used in the offence, and Kasera was produced before a court while further investigation continues.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Tuesday that he would be willing to return to the post following an outpouring of calls for his reinstatement after resigning last week over extramarital affairs, including with an executive of a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls. Huang posted a statement on X saying that if the Board of Directors decides his return is in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company, and America, he would be honored to answer those calls and return as CEO. It was his first public statement since resigning Thursday over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang sounded contrite, saying he did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, that he made serious mistakes in his personal life, that he created problems for the Board that he deeply regrets, and that he owns his mistakes completely while committing to cooperate with the Board's independent investigation. He noted seeing an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers since his departure.

The turmoil has battered shares in Nvidia, which until recently was the world's most valuable publicly traded company. Tech tycoon Elon Musk and other major AI investors have called for Huang's reinstatement with an open letter that has garnered more than 190,000 signatures. US President Donald Trump also signaled his support on Monday for Huang's return, who has advised him on AI policy and is perhaps the tech industry's most recognized promoter of artificial intelligence.

US lawmakers said Tuesday that Huang will appear before three US House committees on December 1 for questioning over concerns that China was able to gain access to advanced US chips from Nvidia. The named subjects associated with these quantities include Jensen Huang, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation, Elon Musk, and the open letter signed by more than 190,000 people.
items.title: Huang Says Willing To Return As Nvidia CEO

A scandal engulfed American chipmaker Nvidia after revelations that its co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang had extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. US intelligence officials reportedly concluded that Alice Huang — an executive linked to Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed International — had been funnelning information to Beijing, while Megaspeed was suspected of steering Nvidia AI chips into China. The allegations drew sharp denials from China's foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun, who dismissed them as baseless smearing, and prompted Beijing to accuse the United States of using spying claims as a pretext for a technological blockade.

The fallout accelerated in late October when Trump voiced support for Huang while noting Washington was looking closely at the matter. On November 9, Nvidia's board announced it had opened a probe after Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair and expressed that he was deeply sorry. The stock market reaction was severe: Nvidia shares fell as much as eight percent during trading, wiping out around $300 billion in market value, with the share price later plunging by around 28 percent since the scandal began.

Legal and political pressure mounted quickly. US-based Rosen Law Firm filed a class-action lawsuit accusing Huang and Nvidia of failing to disclose information about his links to the suspected spy. On November 16, Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive with immediate effect, prompting interim CEO Colette Kress to lead while the board searched for a successor; Trump suggested former Apple boss Tim Cook should take over.

Congressional scrutiny followed, with US lawmakers summoning Huang in December — including public testimony before a Senate committee on December 3 and a closed-door House hearing on December 1. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was also set to testify amid reports that his department may have failed to act on suspicions about Megaspeed rerouting Nvidia technology.

In response, the Trump administration announced tougher export controls on AI chips aimed at closing loopholes allowing Chinese companies remote access to Nvidia's technology. Under the new rules, data centres worldwide would need US licences to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to firms headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under arms embargoes; operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil likewise required licensing.

The open letter campaign for Huang's reinstatement gathered more than 158,000 signatories including tech figures such as Elon Musk. Meanwhile, Megaspeed confirmed Alice Huang had left the company over a year ago with no current role, said it was investigating its compliance with export controls and would cooperate transparently with US authorities; Malaysian authorities were separately probing Speedmatrix, a local subsidiary of Megaspeed.

The article notes that Nvidia's share price on Wall Street has plunged by around 28 percent since the scandal began in late October. (Source: AFP.)
items.title: Nvidia AI-Spy Scandal: Timeline of Key Events

items.summary: Days after stepping down as Nvidia's head over his admission of a personal affair, Jensen Huang has signalled that he is open to leading the chipmaker once more. In his first public remarks since leaving the company, Huang said he had been urged by employees, investors, partners and customers to take up the CEO role again if the board felt his return would serve shareholders, staff, the firm and the country well. Writing on X on Tuesday, November 17, Huang thanked those who stood by him and his family over the past week, saying their support meant the world to him. He acknowledged serious errors in his private life, admitting he had fallen short of the standards expected at Nvidia and that he created problems for the Board that he deeply regrets. Huang stated he owns his mistakes completely and is committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation. In a message posted on X, he reflected on having come to the United States 53 years ago, calling becoming an American citizen one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of his life, and described NVIDIA as his life's work built alongside colleagues into the company it is today. He emphasized that nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible, expressing love for both his country and the firm. Huang said he would return as CEO if the Board decides his reinstatement serves shareholders, employees, the company and America. His willingness to return comes even as Nvidia's board was reported by Fox News not to be considering bringing back the former chief executive to lead the multi-trillion-dollar chipmaker; however, US President Donald Trump has expressed openness to Huang's reinstatement, saying he would not mind seeing him return as CEO and suggesting the Nvidia co-founder had learned a big lesson.
items.title: Jensen Huang Signals Openness to Returning as Nvidia CEO After Stepping Down Over Personal Affair

The article explains that members no longer need to log into the EPFO portal each time they want to check their provident fund account details; instead, these services can be accessed through the EPFO’s WhatsApp channel. To use it, users send 'hi' or 'Hi' to the number +91 87964 41800—or scan a QR code from an EPFO poster on X—and then select their preferred language before choosing Download Passbook and entering the OTP sent to their registered mobile number. The passbook contains details of the member’s provident fund account along with transaction-related entries, and its PDF password is the user’s date of birth.

Beyond downloading a passbook, the WhatsApp service lets members check their EPF balance and view their last five EPF transactions, replacing an earlier SMS-based method. The same services are also available through the UMANG App, which handles everything from generating and activating a UAN to checking balances and downloading passbooks.

The piece then explains what the EPF is: a retirement scheme for organised-sector employees in which both employee and employer contribute up to 12% of monthly basic salary plus dearness allowance each month. Of that contribution, while the entire 12% from the employee goes into the PF account, only 3.67% of the employer’s 12% is invested there; the remaining 8.33% funds the Employees’ Pension Scheme (EPS), but only when the member belongs to both EPF and EPS.

Finally, it defines a UAN as a 12-digit permanent account number allotted by the EPFO that acts as an umbrella identifier linking multiple member IDs across different jobs.
items.title: How to Access EPFO Services via WhatsApp and Understand PF Contribution Structure

items.summary: The Jammu & Kashmir government announced that it is set to reserve 25% of seats in the entry-level class of private unaided schools for children from economically weaker sections (EWS) and disadvantaged groups, implementing this under Section 12(1)(c) of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009. The decision was made by Education minister Shamim Firdous during a meeting with representatives of private school associations, parents' associations, and civil society members in Srinagar on Tuesday. She stated that the rules governing RTE Section 12(1)(c) implementation are in their final stage and that a notification will be issued shortly. The initiative aims to promote inclusive education, ensure equitable access to quality schooling, and extend greater educational opportunities to children from underprivileged backgrounds. Additionally, the government will reimburse schools for admissible expenditure incurred on implementing the scheme.
items.title: Jammu & Kashmir to Mandate EWS Quota in Private School Entry Classes

items.summary: The Indian Ministry of External Affairs condemned a missile attack on the Panama-flagged LPG tanker MT TARA GAS, which occurred on 16 November 2026 while carrying 24 Indian nationals through the Strait of Hormuz. The ministry reported that 21 of those seafarers had been safely evacuated ashore at Khasab and admitted to hospital as injured, with one Indian national still missing following a subsequent attack that forced the crew to abandon the vessel. India's Embassy in Oman was closely monitoring search and rescue operations in coordination with Omani authorities, while appreciating the timely assistance extended by the Government of Oman.
items.title: Indian Seafarers Injured and One Missing After Tanker Attack in Strait of Hormuz

items.summary: Federal Reserve official Barr delivered remarks following the US Federal Reserve's latest Financial Stability Report, released on Friday, which found that 87% of surveyed contacts identified artificial intelligence as a significant risk to the financial system. The concerns cited included AI-powered cyberattacks, complex financing arrangements, and the possibility that a slowdown in AI-related earnings could trigger a broader stock market decline. Barr highlighted additional risks, noting that widespread reliance on AI-driven trading models could encourage herd behaviour and amplify market volatility, while self-learning algorithms might potentially manipulate markets and create financial instability. He also raised concerns about growing use of AI agents in retail banking, warning that banks may struggle to determine whether an AI system accessing or operating customer accounts has received proper authorisation. Even legitimate AI agents acting on behalf of customers could accelerate bank runs by moving money at unprecedented speeds, potentially overwhelming traditional safeguards, the report stated. Barr's comments were prepared for delivery in Milan, Italy, ahead of a conference at the San Francisco Federal Reserve, where Fed Chair Kevin Warsh was scheduled to convene AI developers, business leaders and academics to discuss the technology's implications for productivity, employment and the broader economy.
items.title: Fed's Barr flags AI risks to financial stability, warns of market disruption

The National Security Agency is experiencing an outage affecting a classified computer network it uses for internal communications and other daily work functions, according to a U.S. official and another person familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the issue. The network, known as NSA Net, has been down since at least early Tuesday morning. Some staff have been unable to access their workplace systems, prompting the agency to instruct some employees to delay arriving at its headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland. A U.S. official said the outage occurred during scheduled routine maintenance and that the agency remained able to conduct mission-critical functions, supported by multiple layers of system redundancy designed to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events. The article does not identify a more specific technical cause.

The NSA did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment, though CNN had earlier reported the outage. In related context, U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC before the NSA issue was reported that recent technology failures were not the result of a cyberattack. A series of technology failures have brought down critical systems and disrupted operations around the world in recent weeks: a technical glitch at JPMorgan Chase & Co. on Monday caused some customers' transactions to take longer to process, an issue tied to a software bug rather than cybersecurity; United Airlines reported that a technology problem involving its aging communications infrastructure impacted departing flights; Microsoft Corp.'s productivity software was hobbled for roughly 24 hours last week after a bug triggered a system malfunction during a routine rerouting of user traffic on Nov. 11; and U.S. air traffic was snarled over the weekend when a government contractor encountered problems replacing outdated copper wire at a remote location in Arkansas.
items.title: NSA Classified Network Outage Amid Wave of Technology Failures

In the first nine months of 2026, Bangladesh's apparel exports to the European Union fell sharply year-on-year. Reported figures place the decline at about 11.91%, reducing export value to roughly EUR 13.48 billion and cutting Bangladesh's share of EU apparel imports by value from around 21.1% in the prior period to approximately 19.06%. This made Bangladesh the worst-performing supplier among the EU's 11 largest apparel exporters, with an estimated loss of about EUR 1.82 billion during the nine-month span.

The contraction reflected weakness across two dimensions: shipment volumes reportedly fell by around 5.74%, while the average export value per kilogram dropped roughly 6.54% to approximately EUR 13.70, significantly below the EU's average apparel import price of about EUR 19.59 per kilogram—underscoring pricing pressure on Bangladeshi exporters.

The pace varied across sub-periods: export value fell around 20.89% in January-April, narrowed to roughly 1.25% between May and August, then accelerated again with a decline of about 9.49% in September alone—concerning because overall EU apparel imports contracted only modestly by approximately 2.72% during that month.

In contrast, China strengthened its position as the EU's largest apparel supplier over January-September, with exports reportedly rising around 4.46% year-on-year to about EUR 24.25 billion and shipment volumes up roughly 6.38%. Consequently, China's share of EU apparel imports increased to approximately 34.29%, from around 32.02% in the corresponding prior period.

The divergent trajectories highlight intensifying competitive pressure on Bangladesh's garment sector as rival suppliers gain ground in one of its most important export markets.
items.title: Bangladesh Apparel Exports to EU Fall Nearly 12% as China Gains Market Share: What Went Wrong?
